newsitem.title: INDIA: Hint of risk ahead for Indian rupee.
newsitem.headline: Hint of risk ahead for Indian rupee.

text.p: A senior Indian central banker's verdict tt the rupee is overvalued is unlikely to shake a stubbornly firm spot rate, but there was a broad hint to corporates and importers to start covering forward positions, foreign exchange dealers told Reuters on Sunday.

Y.V. Reddy, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), told an annual conference of the Forex Association of India that the rupee was overvalued based on real effective exchange rate index measures.

The rupee, surfing on inflows of foreign capital attracted by a liberalising economy and the best performing stock market in Asia this year, has held its own against a dollar which is top dog elsewhere on international exchanges.

The rupee has been stable between 35.70/85 for the past year. It closed on Thursday at 35.7125/75 to the dollar. Markets were shut on Friday for the country's celebration of 50 years of independence from colonial rule.
Only persistent intervention by the central bank has stopped the runaway rupee, and India's foreign exchange reserves have risen to all time highs of nearly $30 billion.

Reddy foresaw a natural correction in the spot rate once oil companies begin repaying short term loans they borrowed to cover feedstock purchases while waiting for the authorities to reimburse them some $4.3 billion for selling petroleum products at subsidised rates.
He also said a pick up in industrial growth, when it comes, will feed demand for dollars.
But importers and corporates have become complacent about covering their exposures becaue of the steady rupee-dollar rate, which acts as a disincentive to paying the forward premia.
"This is a warning to all those unhedged positions held by corporates," said an Indian bank dealer. "If it (dollar-rupee) moves there will be a huge demand for forward cover."
Another senior RBI official said the players should be prepared. "Exchange markets are there to cover risks," he told the conference.

Meantime, delegates leaving the conference, which ended Saturday, said there was nothing said that would alter their trading strategies, and the rupee would be judged on the RBI's interventions not its words.
The prevailing market dynamics are too stark to start second guessing when the pressure building up will break the rupee's surface calm.

"As long as capital inflows are going to be more than the trade deficit the rupee is going to remain strong," Moses Harding, chief dealer at IndusInd Bank Ltd, told Reuters Financial Television on the first day of the two day meet.
But there is a growing perception that the rupee's strength is becoming too hot to handle.
The central bank's net purchases of dollars totalled $7.8 billion in 1996/97 (April-March) and in the first four months of this fiscal year totted up to $4.6 billion.

The extra rupees in circulation because of the dollar buying is causing problems controlling money supply, which running at 16.7 percent annually for M3 growth, Reddy termed as in the upper tolerance limits.
And buying dollars and then sucking the rupees entering the system back out of circulation through government debt sales carried a cost for India of around five percent.
The dollars bought by the RBI are deposited with the U.S. Federal Reserve, where they earn six percent, while the yield payable on the government paper is between 11 and 12 percent, dealers noted.
